name: Koireng
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Singh, Chungkham Yashwanta. 2010. Koireng Grammar. New Delhi: Akansha (verified via OpenLibrary; no online text).

new_statements.quote: Sadu Koireng belongs to register tone where tone marking in the lexical items is steady throughout as opposed to contours where the essential feature is changing pitch. Therefore this language belongs to register tone. [p. 101:] This language has level and falling tones. In this study, level tones are left unmarked and falling are marked as [\]. These two tones constitute the two different tonemes occurring in contrasting positions. The following examples illustrate this point. level / falling: ha 'teeth' / ha 'that'; luŋ 'heart' / luŋ 'stone'; caŋ 'paddy' / caŋ 'net'; thi 'blood' / thi 'dead'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The source describes Sadu Koireng as a register-tone language with two contrastive tonemes (level vs falling) on the syllable, illustrated with monosyllabic minimal pairs. It says nothing at all about word stress or accent: the words 'stress' and 'accent' occur nowhere in the thesis. No stress placement rule can be extracted.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the tone section is three pages and gives only monosyllabic minimal pairs. No polysyllabic tone or prominence patterns are described.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is stated to be a property of the syllable, marked on the vowel nucleus; examples are monosyllabic citation forms. Chapter 5 mentions 'rising intonation' only as a means of forming yes/no questions (5.6.1), a sentence-level matter.
new_statements.identity_note: The opened primary source describes Sadu Koireng, the variety of Sadu village, Senapati district, Manipur (about 30 km from Imphal), cross-checked with a second Sadu speaker; Glottolog has no separate dialect code, so it falls under koir1240. Koireng = Koren = Kolren (Grierson's 'Kolren or Koireng', Old Kuki). Glottolog's alternate-name list for koir1240 also carries Liangmai/Liyang/Kwoireng names; Grierson explicitly separates Kwoireng/Liyang (Naga-Kuki group; Liangmai lian1251) from Kolren/Koireng, so those names should not be read as this language.

sources.note: Chapter 2 'Phonological system of the language' (pp. 30-103) covers vowels, consonants, clusters, syllable (2.11, pp. 90-99) and tone (2.12, pp. 100-103). The words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur anywhere in the thesis (grep of all chapters); the language is described as having two register tones, level vs falling (p. 101). No statement on word stress.

sources.note: Sociolinguistic survey. Koireng entry (section 6, pp. 94-95) gives region, population 1410 (2001 census), alternate names Kwoireng/Koireng/Kolren/Koren, Grierson's Old Kuki classification and language use. Nothing on phonology, stress or tone.

sources.citation: Grierson, G. A. (ed.). 1904. Linguistic Survey of India, vol. III pt. III (Tibeto-Burman family: Kuki-Chin and Burma groups), 'Kolren or Koireng', pp. 234-241. Calcutta.
sources.note: 'Pronunciation' paragraph (p. 234) discusses only indistinct prefix vowels, vowel and consonant interchanges and silent finals; nothing on accent, stress or tone. Based on two specimens and a wordlist by Babu Bisharup Singh, Kharang Koireng village.
